current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually consistent answer includes all semantically required visual elements directly necessary to answer the question’s literal, narrow intent — and only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with unambiguous visual evidence. It is not applicable to: (1) binary, yes/no, or single-attribute questions (e.g., ‘Is this a red car?’ or ‘What color is the text?’ — completeness only applies if the question demands a multi-element visual inventory); (2) interpretive, inferential, or subjective questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’ or ‘What is the object’s purpose?’); (3) questions requiring spatial or compositional inference unless visually confirmed (e.g., ‘between’, ‘enclosing’, or ‘sandwiched’); (4) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect calibrated uncertainty or question relevance. Completeness is a tiebreaker metric only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and in such cases, the answer that includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible text, logos, objects, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission is preferred — even if more verbose. It does not penalize inclusion of contextually relevant, visually verifiable details (e.g., background objects, peripheral notes) — only omission of elements that are semantically required to fulfill the question’s literal intent. ‘Semantically required’ means elements directly necessary to answer the question’s core visual inventory demand — e.g., for ‘What is on the table?’, completeness requires listing all visible items on the table — not every object in the room; for ‘Describe the composition’, completeness requires including foreground/background, relative positioning, and compositional framing — even if not the primary subject; for ‘What is the text?’, completeness requires including all visible text — even if not directly referenced — if it is visually present and semantically relevant to the question. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table; ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors; ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory; ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory; ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element; ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must not apply completeness to hallucinated or visually unsupported claims — even if plausible — and must not penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — only for omission of semantically required elements. The criterion is not a tool to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers — only between factually correct, visually grounded answers. The description must unambiguously exclude any question type not meeting the above criteria — including subjective, inferential, or ambiguous questions — and must explicitly state that completeness is only a tiebreaker for inventory-style questions with clear visual evidence. Workers must not assume that all visible visual elements are ‘semantically relevant’ — only those directly required to answer the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also avoid penalizing factual, verifiable details that are visually present and directly relevant to the question’s literal intent — even if they are not the ‘primary’ answer. The description must clearly state that for binary classification or posture-based questions, the visual distinction (e.g., ‘legs bent’) is semantically required — and that omission of such a detail, even if not the ‘main point’, reduces completeness. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘unnecessary detail’ refers to non-essential, contextually irrelevant information — not factual, visually verifiable details that are critical to answering the question’s literal intent.

current_criteria.name: consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually consistent answer’s non-visual inferences — such as inferred activity, material behavior, symbolic meaning, or contextual function — are logically coherent with real-world knowledge or domain-specific facts, but only when those inferences are minimally speculative and directly supported by the visual context. It does NOT apply to literal visual claims (e.g., object identity, color, position, count, or attribute state) — which are evaluated under visual grounding and factual consistency. This criterion is ONLY invoked AFTER visual fidelity is confirmed — any answer that misrepresents the image is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image and cannot be assessed here. It is also inapplicable when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in such cases, workers must defer to other criteria (e.g., clarity, specificity) and must not penalize plausible, minimally inferential claims. When visual evidence is clear and unambiguous, the answer must first be visually accurate — only then can domain plausibility be assessed. If two answers are equally visually grounded and factually consistent, this criterion may be used as a tiebreaker — but only for non-hallucinatory, minimally speculative inferences (e.g., ‘the person is likely browsing Apple-related pages’ based on visible screen content — not fabricating non-visible details like ‘the person is wearing a jersey’). Hallucinations (invented visual content) are always disqualifying — even if plausible — and must be penalized under factual_consistency_with_the_image. Domain knowledge alignment is not a substitute for visual fidelity — it cannot override or validate visually unsupported claims. The criterion does not penalize plausible inferences that are grounded in the visual context — even if they are not explicitly stated — as long as they are not hallucinations. It also does not evaluate aesthetic, subjective, or interpretive descriptions — those are not domain knowledge claims. If a claim is visually supported and domain-plausible, it is preferred — but if it is visually incorrect, it is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion should not be used to resolve ties when one answer is visually incorrect — the visually correct answer must be preferred. Workers must prioritize visual fidelity over domain plausibility — even if a claim is ‘more common-sense’ or ‘more plausible’. The criterion is not applicable to questions asking for literal, positional, or count-based claims — and should be avoided for yes/no or binary questions unless visual evidence is unambiguous. Examples of valid applications: ‘The hydrant is silver because it is made of metal’ (material plausibility) or ‘The person is likely a skater’ (contextual logic — based on visible posture and environment). Examples of invalid applications: ‘There is a giraffe in the image’ (visually unsupported) or ‘The person is wearing a team jersey’ (visually unsupported). Workers must not use this criterion to penalize visually correct answers for being ‘less plausible’ or ‘less common-sense’ — and must not apply it to hallucinated or speculative claims — even if plausible. The criterion is not a gatekeeper — it is only a tiebreaker when visual fidelity is equal, and only for grounded, minimally speculative inferences. The description must explicitly state that this criterion is never applied to visually misrepresentative claims — even if they are domain-plausible — and that visual grounding is the sole gatekeeper. Workers must not use domain knowledge to validate or override visual facts — even if the inference is common-sense. The criterion is not about style or tone — only about logical coherence with domain knowledge — and should be applied conservatively, only when visual evidence clearly supports an inference. This criterion is only applicable to non-visual inferences — not to visual misrepresentations — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation if visual evidence is misrepresented or omitted. It is not a tool to penalize or validate domain plausibility in visually incorrect answers — and must be applied only to non-literal, contextually grounded inferences — not to visual facts or misrepresentations.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: The answer must strictly align with visually verifiable content in the image — including object identities, locations, states, counts, and spatial relationships — without misrepresenting, inventing, or omitting critical visual evidence that is materially relevant to the question’s intent. This criterion applies only to questions that explicitly demand literal, measurable, or verifiable visual facts — such as object identification, spatial positioning, attribute states, or count-based claims — and does NOT apply to interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, or stylistic questions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘composition’, ‘intent’, ‘aesthetic effect’), which are evaluated under other criteria. Workers must evaluate every claim against the image’s direct, unambiguous visual evidence — not external knowledge, assumptions, or plausible inferences — and must visually inspect and confirm every claim (including text, logos, colors, textures, and spatial relationships) with absolute precision. Hallucinations (invented objects, misidentified attributes, misattributed elements, or false claims about non-existent visual content) are disqualifying errors — regardless of plausibility — and must be penalized equally, without severity ranking. If visual evidence is unambiguous, no uncertainty is allowed — even if the claim is speculative or inferential. If visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded, the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., 'appears to be', 'likely', 'based on visual evidence') — not invent details. Omitting non-critical details is acceptable — but omitting visually present, materially relevant elements (e.g., objects, text, spatial anchors) is a factual error. Claims about object mounting, structural attachment, or functional attributes must be directly verifiable — not inferred. Spatial claims (e.g., 'centered', 'near the edge', 'above', 'straight', 'curved', 'consistent spacing') must be evaluated using frame boundaries, area proportions, and relative positioning — not subjective interpretation — and must be verified independently: 'consistent spacing' is a factual claim requiring visual verification, not an inference about organizational pattern. Misidentifications (e.g., mistaking a horse for a donkey) are hallucinations if they misrepresent visual evidence — and must be penalized. All claims must be anchored to concrete, measurable visual evidence — not abstract or inferential descriptions. The criterion does not apply to stylistic, contextual, or domain-specific interpretations — those are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’. If visual evidence contradicts external knowledge, the visual evidence must prevail — even if it is counterintuitive. Workers must not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The answer must not rely on context, branding, or brand association to make claims about visual content — only direct visual evidence. Text, logos, and visible attributes (e.g., 'Coca-Cola' text, red color, 'Answers' label) must be verified visually — not assumed or inferred. Claims about operating systems or software must be verifiable via UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos. All claims must be grounded in visual plausibility — not abstract reasoning. If visual evidence is insufficient to confirm or deny a claim, the answer must reflect uncertainty — not make speculative assertions. If both answers are factually consistent, the more complete or accurate visual description is preferred — but never at the cost of introducing hallucinations. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for hypothetical, biological, or non-visual interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. If a claim is visually verifiable — even if negative or partial — it is factually consistent. Absolute denials (e.g., 'no one is wearing jerseys') must be verified — and if false, they are penalized — but if true, they are not. All hallucinations are equally disqualifying — no severity ranking is allowed. Workers must trust the image over assumptions, even if the image is ambiguous or misinterpreted. If visual evidence is clear, any misrepresentation is a hallucination — regardless of how plausible it may seem. If both answers contain hallucinations, mark both as incorrect — or if forced to choose, the answer with fewer hallucinations is preferred — but only after verifying that the hallucinations are clearly distinguishable. The criterion does not apply to external factual claims (e.g., artist attribution, title, provenance) unless those claims are visually verifiable (e.g., visible signature, title on canvas). Workers should evaluate only claims directly observable in the image — not external metadata. If the question asks for a description of the image’s content, the answer may include contextual facts — but if not visually present, they are not required and should not be penalized for omission. Visual descriptions (e.g., color, object type) are evaluated based on visual plausibility and context — not strict technical terminology. If multiple object labels are visually plausible (e.g., 'jet ski' vs 'water scooter'), the answer that is more visually accurate in composition, positioning, and color should be preferred — even if it uses a less precise term. Object identification errors are disqualifying, but color or spatial description errors are only penalized if they are clearly false or hallucinated — and visual composition and spatial relationships should be prioritized over precise terminology. Spatial relationships must be evaluated based on visual perspective — not subjective interpretation. Hallucinations include misplacement of objects, misattribution of visual elements, and false claims about non-existent visual content. All claims must be visually grounded — even if the visual evidence is partially obscured or low-resolution — and workers must not assume or infer visual content. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether needles are 'icy' or 'cold'), the answer must reflect uncertainty — but if the visual evidence is unambiguous, no such ambiguity exists, and any misrepresentation must be rejected. If a claim is visually unsupported (e.g., 'half-squatting'), it must be marked as such or avoided — not assumed. Visual grounding and factual consistency are interdependent — and ambiguity or inference must be clearly qualified — not assumed. All claims must be verified — regardless of their type. If both answers are factually inconsistent, the one with fewer unsupported claims (even if more severe) should be selected — or both should be marked incorrect — but never that a misidentification is 'less' inconsistent than a hallucination if both are visually unsupported. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates whether an answer includes only minimally necessary, measurable, and visually verifiable visual details that directly and precisely fulfill the question’s intent — and only when the question explicitly demands or benefits from such precision (e.g., ‘where’, ‘how many’, ‘relative position’, ‘size’, ‘color’, ‘text’, or ‘attribute state’). It is NOT applicable to abstract, interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, or inferential questions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘intent’, ‘purpose’, ‘function’, or ‘what is this object doing?’), which are evaluated under other criteria. Specificity is a tiebreaker metric only when both answers are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — and only for questions that require measurable visual precision. Any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or visually unsupported claims is disqualified from specificity evaluation — even if more detailed — and must be penalized under factual_consistency_with_the_image first. Workers must evaluate specificity only after confirming visual grounding and factual consistency — and if one answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, specificity is not applicable. Specificity rewards grounded precision — not verbosity, irrelevant detail, or speculative claims — and includes multi-element descriptions (e.g., ‘the red car is left of the tree, behind the fence’) as long as all elements are visually verifiable and non-hallucinatory. It does not penalize contextually grounded, minimally inferential descriptions (e.g., ‘provides ground coverage’, ‘indicates indoor setting’) if they are visually plausible — as long as they do not hallucinate or misrepresent visual evidence. Specificity does not apply to linguistic, semantic, or abstract factual claims (e.g., brand names, software inferences) — unless those claims are directly verifiable via visual attributes (e.g., ‘the logo is red’ or ‘the text says ‘macOS’’). When visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, workers must mark the answer as uncertain — and specificity is not evaluated in such cases. Specificity is not a standalone metric — it is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and should not be used to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers. It is not applicable to binary or simple factual questions (e.g., yes/no) — which are evaluated under other criteria. Specificity does not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations — and should not be used to penalize factually correct, contextually rich answers for being ‘less literal’. Workers must prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency over specificity — even if an answer appears more precise — and must reject any answer that is hallucinated — regardless of how plausible or detailed it is. Specificity is not a tool to validate or reward detail — only to compare precision among factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must be applied conservatively, only when the question’s intent requires measurable visual attributes. Examples: ‘The red car is to the left of the tree’ (valid specificity) vs. ‘The red car is to the left of the tree and smells like roses’ (invalid due to unsupported detail). ‘The dog has a brown collar’ (valid) vs. ‘The dog is barking’ (invalid if not visually verifiable). Specificity should not be applied to aesthetic or compositional descriptions — even if they are visually grounded — unless the question explicitly asks for visual composition or structure analysis — in which case, such descriptions are evaluated under contextual_relevance_of_visual_elements and visual_stability_under_transformation — not under specificity. The criterion must be applied only to questions that demand quantifiable visual attributes — and must exclude any question that requires inferential, causal, or contextual explanation — even if visually grounded — unless it explicitly demands measurable visual precision. Workers must not use specificity to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must not apply it to questions where precision is not explicitly required or where the answer is factually incorrect. Specificity is not a gatekeeper — it is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and even then, only for questions that explicitly require measurable visual precision — and must be applied only after visual grounding and factual consistency are verified.

current_criteria.name: temporal_consistency_of_visual_elements
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer maintains coherent and accurate descriptions of visual elements across time — applicable only to questions involving explicit sequences, video frames, or multi-frame comparisons (e.g., ‘what changes between frames?’, ‘how does the object move?’, ‘what happens next?’). Workers must verify that claims about motion, state change, or spatial evolution are temporally consistent with the visual evidence — and must penalize any hallucinated, invented, or misrepresentative claims about transitions — even if the visual content is otherwise factually correct. This criterion is inapplicable to static images or questions without temporal context (e.g., ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe the composition’, ‘what is the object’s color?’), and workers must explicitly mark it as inapplicable in such cases — deferring to factual_consistency_with_the_image and visual grounding for evaluation. When applicable, temporal consistency is the sole metric — with no fallback to other criteria — and workers must not use it to penalize vagueness, cautious phrasing, or semantic drift. If both answers are factually consistent and visually grounded under this criterion, the answer with better temporal coherence is preferred — but only if the question explicitly involves motion, state change, or visual evolution across time. Workers must reject any answer that invents motion or state transitions not supported by the sequence — even if plausible — and must not apply this criterion to static images, aesthetic descriptions, or inferential claims about current state. It does not apply to metaphorical or compositional use of motion (e.g., ‘the scene flows’), which are allowed as long as they are grounded in visual structure — not hallucinated transitions. The criterion must be strictly limited to multi-frame or temporal contexts — and workers must confirm the question’s intent before evaluation — with no tolerance for misapplication.

current_criteria.name: visual_stability_under_transformation
current_criteria.description: Evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually consistent answer’s claims remain valid under minor, realistic image transformations (e.g., rotation, zoom, cropping, or color shift) — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. Applicable ONLY to questions that explicitly demand descriptions of visually invariant properties: object identity, intrinsic attributes (color, material, shape), or structural relationships (e.g., ‘this is a circle’, ‘the object is red’, ‘the text says ‘Apple’’). Workers must verify that the answer’s claims are objectively unchanged under such transformations — i.e., they would still be true even if the image were rotated or cropped — assuming the visual content remains intact. This criterion does NOT apply to: (1) spatial, contextual, or framing-dependent claims (e.g., ‘on the left’, ‘near the window’, ‘foreground’), (2) interpretive, aesthetic, or subjective descriptions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘composition’), (3) dynamic or motion-related claims (e.g., ‘moving’, ‘falling’), (4) questions requiring identification of specific individuals, roles, or contextual positions (e.g., ‘who is this person?’, ‘what is the role?’), (5) questions asking for presence/absence, visibility, or binary factual claims (e.g., ‘is there a dog?’), or (6) questions asking for detailed visual descriptions unless explicitly demanding invariant properties. The criterion is NOT a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually correct and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding before assessing stability — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion. Stability is evaluated only for claims that are inherently invariant — e.g., object identity or color — and does NOT penalize factually correct, visually grounded descriptions of position or context — even if they are frame-dependent. Workers must NOT penalize grounded, non-hallucinated descriptions for being ‘fragile’ or ‘context-dependent’ — only for misrepresenting visual content. The criterion should be applied conservatively — only when the question’s intent is to evaluate robust, invariant visual properties — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for descriptive, interpretive, or contextually grounded questions. Workers must evaluate whether the answer’s claims would remain factually correct under reasonable transformations — and if they would not, the answer is penalized — even if it is factually correct under the original image. The criterion is not a substitute for factual accuracy — it is a secondary validation for invariant properties — and must not override factual correctness. Workers must avoid conflating ‘visual stability’ with ‘visual robustness’ or ‘visual distinctness’ — and must evaluate only claims that are objectively unchanged under transformations — not subjective interpretations. The criterion is not applicable to questions asking for screen content, UI state, or text interpretation — even if those claims are visually stable — because they are not structurally invariant — and must be evaluated under other criteria (e.g., visual grounding or factual consistency). Workers must not use this criterion to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘less stable’ — and must not apply it to questions that are not visual in nature — or to questions that do not explicitly demand invariant properties. The criterion is designed to identify and penalize hallucinations or misrepresentations that become false under transformation — not to evaluate the quality of contextual or spatial descriptions — even if those descriptions are factually correct.

current_criteria.name: avoidance_of_ambiguous_visual_references
current_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids ambiguous or vague visual references (e.g., 'a red thing', 'the object on the left', 'something in the background') that could refer to multiple or indeterminate visual elements. Applicable only when the image contains multiple visually similar or indistinct objects, or when the question requires precise visual identification. Workers must verify whether the answer uses unambiguous visual anchors (e.g., 'the red car with the blue stripe', 'the person holding the sign', 'the object in the bottom-left quadrant') — avoiding generic or contextually ambiguous terms. This criterion does not apply to subjective, aesthetic, or interpretive questions — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. It is not a tiebreaker — only used to evaluate factually consistent, visually grounded answers — and penalizes ambiguity even if the answer is otherwise correct. Workers must evaluate whether the answer’s visual references are uniquely identifiable — and penalize answers that rely on ambiguous or potentially misleading phrasing.

current_criteria.name: accuracy_of_visual_interpretation
current_criteria.description: Assesses whether the answer’s interpretation of visual content aligns with the image’s literal, observable evidence — without introducing misinterpretations or over-extrapolations that go beyond what is visually present. Applicable only when the question requires interpretation of visual context, structure, or composition — e.g., ‘what does this suggest?’, ‘how is this arranged?’, or ‘what is the relationship?’. Workers must verify whether the interpretation is grounded in verifiable visual elements — e.g., if the answer claims ‘the person is gesturing toward the exit’, the visual evidence must support the direction and posture — not inferred intent. This criterion does not apply to literal object identification or spatial claims — which are evaluated under visual grounding and factual consistency. It is not a tiebreaker — only used to evaluate factually consistent, visually grounded answers — and penalizes misinterpretations even if plausible. Workers must evaluate whether the interpretation is directly supported by visual evidence — and penalize claims that misrepresent visual context or over-infer non-visual intent.

current_criteria.name: coherence_of_logical_flow
current_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer’s visual description follows a logically structured and coherent sequence — ensuring that the visual claims are presented in a way that supports the question’s intent without introducing contradictory or disjointed claims. Applicable only when the question requires multi-step or multi-element visual reasoning — e.g., ‘describe the scene from left to right’, ‘what is the sequence of events?’, or ‘what are the relationships between objects?’. Workers must verify whether the answer’s structure supports logical progression — e.g., spatial, causal, or compositional flow — without introducing contradictions or disjointed claims. This criterion does not apply to single-element or literal description questions — which are evaluated under specificity or visual grounding. It is not a tiebreaker — only used to evaluate factually consistent, visually grounded answers — and penalizes logical disarray even if the content is correct. Workers must evaluate whether the visual description’s structure supports the question’s intent — and penalize answers that present claims in a confusing or illogical order.

current_criteria.name: appropriateness_of_verbosity_level
current_criteria.description: Assesses whether the answer’s level of detail is proportionate to the question’s intent — avoiding excessive verbosity that adds no visual value or insufficient verbosity that omits critical visual elements. Applicable only when the question requires a balanced level of detail — e.g., ‘describe the image briefly’ vs. ‘describe the image in detail’. Workers must verify whether the answer’s verbosity matches the question’s scope — e.g., if the question asks for a brief description, the answer should not include exhaustive object inventories; if the question asks for detailed analysis, the answer should not omit critical visual elements. This criterion does not apply to questions that are ambiguous or subjective — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. It is not a tiebreaker — only used to evaluate factually consistent, visually grounded answers — and penalizes verbosity that adds no value or brevity that omits key visual content. Workers must evaluate whether the answer’s verbosity level is appropriate to the question’s intent — and penalize answers that are either overly verbose or overly minimal for the context.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must accurately reflect what is visible in the image — describing objects, positions, colors, textures, and actions as they appear. It should not invent or misrepresent visual elements. Evaluated by direct comparison to the image content.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked, without drifting into irrelevant topics or tangential information. Evaluated by whether the answer’s core focus aligns with the question’s intent.

If a claim is visually unsupported (e.g., 'half-squatting'), it must be marked as such or avoided — not assumed. Visual grounding and factual consistency are interdependent — and ambiguity or inference must be clearly qualified — not assumed. All claims must be verified — regardless of their type. If both answers are factually inconsistent, the one with fewer unsupported claims (even if more severe) should be selected — or both should be marked incorrect — but never that a misidentification is 'less' inconsistent than a hallucination if both are visually unsupported. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer should not include details not present in the image — such as objects, actions, or attributes that are not visible or inferable with high confidence. Evaluated by flagging unsupported or invented visual claims.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether an answer includes all visually verifiable elements that are semantically required by the question’s literal intent — and only when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. A factual error or hallucination disqualifies the answer from completeness evaluation — factual accuracy must be verified first. Completeness does NOT apply to: (1) subjective, interpretive, or inferential questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’, ‘Is this art?’, ‘What is the object’s purpose?’), (2) questions requiring inference beyond direct visual evidence (e.g., ‘between’, ‘enclosing’, or ‘sandwiched’ unless visually confirmed), (3) yes/no or binary questions, (4) questions asking for a single, directly observable attribute (e.g., ‘What color is the text?’ — completeness is only for multi-element inventory tasks), or (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect uncertainty via calibrated uncertainty or question relevance. Completeness is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and in such cases, the answer that includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible text, logos, objects, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission is preferred — even if more verbose. It does not penalize inclusion of non-essential, contextually relevant visual details (e.g., background objects, peripheral notes) — only omission of elements semantically required by the question’s intent. ‘Semantically required’ means elements directly necessary to fulfill the question’s core visual inventory demand — e.g., for ‘What is on the table?’, completeness requires listing all visible items on the table — not every object in the room. For ‘Describe the composition’, completeness requires including foreground/background, relative positioning, and compositional framing — even if not the primary subject. For ‘What is the text?’, completeness requires including all visible text — even if not directly referenced — if it is visually present and semantically relevant to the question. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table. ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors. ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory. ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory. ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element. ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: The answer should provide precise, detailed descriptions (e.g., exact locations, orientations, relative sizes) rather than vague or generalized statements. Evaluated by the level of detail and specificity in spatial or descriptive claims.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should use appropriate qualifiers (e.g., “possibly,” “likely,” “appears to be”) when describing uncertain or inferential content, and avoid overconfidence in unverifiable claims. Evaluated by whether the answer appropriately balances certainty and uncertainty.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be grammatically correct, free of ambiguity, and use straightforward, natural language. Evaluated by readability, clarity, and absence of confusing or convoluted phrasing.

all_criteria.name: accuracy_of_visual_interpretation
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly interprets visual attributes (e.g., color, texture, motion, occlusion, lighting) that are not explicitly labeled but are inferable from the image. Applicable only when the question requires nuanced visual reasoning beyond object identification. Workers must judge whether the interpretation aligns with plausible visual cues — not speculative or artistic rendering. Example: correctly inferring ‘the dog is running’ from blurred motion, or ‘the surface is wet’ from reflections. Accuracy is measured against the most plausible visual interpretation consistent with the image’s evidence. This criterion is distinct from visual grounding (which requires literal presence) and from factual consistency (which requires visual truth). It is not applicable to purely descriptive or binary questions (e.g., ‘Is there a dog?’). A response that misinterprets visual cues (e.g., claiming motion when none is visible) is penalized. It is also not applicable if the visual evidence is ambiguous and multiple interpretations are plausible — in such cases, the answer must reflect uncertainty, and this criterion is not used for scoring.

all_criteria.name: consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s claims align with real-world knowledge, physical plausibility, or domain-specific facts — but only when the visual evidence is clear and unambiguous. It does NOT override visual grounding or factual consistency with the image. If the answer misrepresents what is visually present (e.g., calling a can a box, or claiming a giraffe has wings), it is penalized under visual grounding or factual consistency — not this criterion. This criterion applies ONLY to inferences or descriptions that are logically or factually coherent with real-world knowledge, such as object behavior, anatomical correctness, material plausibility, or contextual logic (e.g., a skateboarder on a ramp, a hydrant being silver). It does NOT apply to: (1) visual interpretations (e.g., color, position, or object count), (2) vague or imprecise phrasing, (3) speculative but plausible assumptions without visual support (e.g., 'holding a frisbee' without visual evidence), or (4) questions that ask for literal visual description. If an answer is factually correct based on the image, even if metaphorical, it is not penalized. If two answers are equally plausible under domain knowledge, preference should be deferred to other criteria. This criterion is inapplicable when visual evidence is ambiguous or when the question is purely descriptive without requiring domain knowledge validation. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over common sense when conflicts arise.

all_criteria.name: coherence_of_logical_flow
all_criteria.description: The answer should present information in a logical, step-by-step manner that connects ideas naturally — especially when multiple visual elements or inferences are involved. Evaluated by whether the reasoning path is smooth and avoids abrupt or disjointed statements.

all_criteria.name: robustness_to_visual_noise
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer remains accurate and grounded even when the visual evidence is degraded, partially occluded, or low-resolution — without relying on speculative or hallucinated details. Applicable only when the image quality is suboptimal or when the question involves ambiguous visual content. A response is preferred if it avoids over-interpreting noisy or incomplete visual cues — e.g., correctly stating ‘object is blurry’ or ‘cannot distinguish’ rather than inventing attributes. This criterion is not applicable to high-fidelity, clear images — only to those with noise, blur, or occlusion. Workers must judge whether the answer’s confidence and content are proportionate to the visual uncertainty — not whether it is more ‘detailed’ or ‘beautiful’.

all_criteria.name: conciseness_without_loss_of_meaning
all_criteria.description: The answer should be as brief as possible while retaining all necessary information — avoiding redundancy or verbose explanations without sacrificing clarity or completeness. Evaluated by whether the response is succinct yet fully informative.

all_criteria.name: appropriateness_of_verbosity_level
all_criteria.description: The answer should match the complexity and expectations of the question — neither overly simplistic for complex questions nor overly verbose for simple ones. Evaluated by whether the response’s length and detail are proportionate to the question’s demands.

all_criteria.name: multi-element_consistency
all_criteria.description: When the question involves multiple objects or relationships, the answer should consistently treat all elements without contradicting or ignoring any — ensuring holistic visual understanding. Evaluated by whether all visual components are addressed and logically unified in the response.

all_criteria.name: clarity_of_language
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer uses unambiguous, precise, and grammatically correct language that is easy to understand — without unnecessary jargon, vague terms, or syntactic errors that could confuse the reader. Applicable only when the answer’s clarity directly affects its interpretability or its ability to be grounded in the visual content. A response is penalized if it contains ambiguous phrasing (e.g., ‘something is on the left’ when the image shows a specific object) or if it uses jargon or idioms that are not clearly explained. It is also penalized if the language introduces confusion (e.g., ‘the red thing’ when the image contains multiple red objects) — even if the answer is factually correct. Clarity is not about verbosity — a concise answer can be clear; a verbose one can be unclear. This criterion is not applicable to poetic, metaphorical, or stylistic responses — only to answers that must be interpretable to accurately ground or evaluate visual content. It is also not applicable when the question is ambiguous — in such cases, preference should be based on visual grounding and factual consistency.

all_criteria.name: visual_stability_under_transformation
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer remains factually consistent and visually grounded when the image undergoes minor transformations (e.g., rotation, zoom, cropping, or color shift) — without introducing hallucinations or misinterpretations. Applicable only when the answer makes claims about visual elements that are invariant under such transformations (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, or attribute states). Workers must verify whether the answer’s content holds under reasonable visual perturbations — e.g., if an answer claims ‘the object is circular’ and the image is rotated, the claim should remain valid. This criterion is not applicable to answers that are context-dependent, subjective, or hallucinated — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. It also does not apply to questions that require interpretation of non-invariant features (e.g., motion, emotion, or temporal states). The criterion is designed to identify answers that rely on superficial or unstable visual cues — penalizing claims that are visually fragile. For example, if an answer claims ‘the red object is on the left’ and the image is cropped to remove the left half, the claim becomes invalid — such answers are penalized. This criterion is only applicable when the question’s intent requires robust visual description — not for aesthetic or interpretive questions. Workers must evaluate whether the answer’s claims are based on structural, invariant properties of the image — not on position, orientation, or framing-dependent details. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers.

all_criteria.name: temporal_consistency_of_visual_elements
all_criteria.description: Assesses whether the answer maintains consistency in describing visual elements across frames or time-dependent visual contexts — applicable only to questions involving sequences, video frames, or multi-frame images (e.g., ‘what happens next?’, ‘how does the object move?’, or ‘what changes between frames?’). Workers must verify whether the answer’s claims about object motion, state change, or spatial evolution are temporally coherent — without hallucinating or misrepresenting visual transitions. This criterion does not apply to static images or questions that do not involve temporal reasoning. It is not applicable to subjective interpretations or aesthetic judgments — only to verifiable visual transitions. The answer must not invent motion or attribute state changes that are not visually present — even if plausible. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must evaluate whether the visual elements’ evolution is consistent with the image’s sequence — and penalize claims that contradict or misrepresent visual transitions.

all_criteria.name: semantic_coherence_of_visual_description
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer’s visual description aligns with the semantic structure of the question — ensuring that the answer’s content logically follows the question’s intent without introducing semantic mismatches or irrelevant visual elements. Applicable only when the question is complex or multi-faceted — e.g., ‘what is the relationship between A and B?’ — and the answer must not misrepresent or misalign the semantic focus. Workers must verify whether the answer’s content matches the question’s semantic scope — e.g., if the question asks about spatial relationships, the answer must not include attribute or emotional descriptions unless directly relevant. This criterion does not apply to questions that are ambiguous or subjective — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. The answer must not introduce semantic drift — e.g., shifting from object identity to emotion without visual justification. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must evaluate whether the visual description’s semantic focus matches the question’s intent — and penalize answers that misalign or drift from the question’s scope.

all_criteria.name: contextual_relevance_of_visual_elements
all_criteria.description: Assesses whether the answer includes only visual elements that are contextually relevant to the question’s intent — excluding irrelevant background, decorative, or non-essential visual content that does not contribute to answering the question. Applicable only when the image contains multiple visual elements — and the question requires precise visual selection or focus. Workers must verify whether the answer’s visual description is contextually focused — e.g., if the question asks about ‘the person in the foreground’, the answer must not include background objects unless directly relevant. This criterion does not apply to questions that are ambiguous or subjective — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. The answer must not introduce irrelevant visual elements — even if they are visually present — unless they are contextually required. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must evaluate whether the visual description’s context is aligned with the question’s scope — and penalize answers that include irrelevant or distracting visual elements.

all_criteria.name: visual_invariant_accuracy
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer’s claims are based on visual properties that are invariant under common image transformations — such as scale, rotation, or lighting — without relying on frame-dependent or context-sensitive visual cues. Applicable only when the question requires describing object identity, structure, or intrinsic properties — e.g., ‘what is the object?’ or ‘what is the material?’. Workers must verify whether the answer’s claims are invariant — e.g., if an answer claims ‘the object is circular’ and the image is rotated, the claim should remain valid. This criterion does not apply to questions that require interpretive or aesthetic judgment — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. The answer must not rely on position, orientation, or framing-dependent visual cues — even if they are visually prominent. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must evaluate whether the visual description’s claims are based on invariant properties — and penalize answers that rely on fragile or context-dependent visual cues.

all_criteria.name: visual_element_abstraction_level
all_criteria.description: Assesses whether the answer’s visual description strikes an appropriate balance between abstraction and concreteness — avoiding overly abstract or overly literal descriptions that misrepresent or oversimplify the visual content. Applicable only when the question requires a nuanced visual interpretation — e.g., ‘describe the composition’ or ‘what does this suggest?’. Workers must verify whether the answer’s level of abstraction matches the question’s intent — e.g., if the question asks for a ‘detailed description’, the answer should not be overly abstract; if the question asks for a ‘high-level summary’, the answer should not be overly literal. This criterion does not apply to questions that are ambiguous or subjective — or when the answer is factually inconsistent — which are disqualified under higher-priority criteria. The answer must not misrepresent the visual content through excessive abstraction or oversimplification — even if it appears plausible. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — it is only used to evaluate answers that are factually consistent and visually grounded — and is not applied to hallucinated or speculative answers. Workers must evaluate whether the visual description’s abstraction level matches the question’s intent — and penalize answers that are too abstract or too literal for the context.

manager_prompt:
List and describe 10 criteria for how human annotators compare the quality of two answers to the same visual question.

The task is RLHF-V style preference comparison for visual question answering and image-text responses. The worker model will receive:
- the image,
- the source question,
- candidate answer A,
- candidate answer B.

Focus on human preference factors such as visual grounding, question relevance, factual consistency with the image, avoidance of hallucinated visual details, completeness, specificity, calibrated uncertainty, and clear language.
